paras: The attempted lynching of Herman Luther took place in Detroit, Michigan, on December 18, 1888, when a street crowd seized and beat Luther moments after he fired a revolver at his divorced wife and children outside the city hall. Police, and by one account the sheriff and his deputies, took Luther away alive before the crowd could hang him. Papers across the country carried the story by wire, several under headlines such as "Nearly Lynched" and "Luther Deserves Lynching."

Luther, described as Prussian by birth and a tailor, had been divorced from his wife, Amelia, and a court had ordered their property sold and the proceeds divided. At the commissioner's sale on Griswold Street, Luther first bid in the property but could not make the required deposit, and Mrs. Luther won it when the sale was reopened. According to the Detroit dispatch carried by the Owosso Times, his wife and children said he had treated them brutally for years and often threatened to kill them.

About 12:30 p.m., as his wife, son and two daughters left the city hall steps, Luther drew a revolver and opened fire. One shot struck his son in the cheek and passed out through the neck, and Luther chased the women up the street, firing as he went. When his daughter fell near the corner of Michigan Avenue, he aimed at her as she lay on the ground, but a bystander seized his arm and the bullet struck a spectator in the leg.

The crowd then turned on Luther. A brick struck him in the face, others wrenched the revolver from him, and the crowd dragged him into the middle of the road amid cries of "lynch him!" and "kill him!" The Owosso Times account adds that men shouted "Get a rope!" and "String him up!" and that one man cut the awning ropes from a nearby store and made a noose. The same account says the arrival of the sheriff, two deputies and a wagon load of policemen saved him from being hanged from a telegraph pole.

Luther was taken in the patrol wagon to the Central Police station, his face and gray hair covered with blood. There he told an officer that he had meant to kill his son and his wife and wished he had done so. His son was expected to recover, and the wounded spectator, a maker of artificial limbs, was said to face the possible loss of his leg. No report of charges against Luther, a trial, or any action against members of the crowd appears in the coverage.

Two versions of a Detroit wire report dated December 18 ran in papers from Connecticut to Montana over the following days. One version ended with the crowd dragging Luther into the road until the patrol wagon arrived, while the other said the crowd was "only prevented from lynching him on the spot" by a large police force. Shorter items reduced the episode to a line, saying Luther "narrowly escaped lynching" or "came near being lynched," and one Wisconsin reprint dropped the crowd's threats entirely.

Headlines focused on Luther's attack on his family, calling him "Mad With Rage" and a "Cowardly Husband and Father," and the St. Paul Daily Globe headed its report "Luther Deserves Lynching." The fullest account, a Detroit dispatch printed in the Owosso Times under "Almost a Lynching," described the crowd as "the leading merchants, bankers, and lawyers" who "did not seem to be aware of what they were doing." A Michigan news column mentioned only the shooting and the "long years of domestic strife" behind it, without the crowd. No paper mentioned race.

Details differ between accounts: the son is named Paul in the Owosso Times and Fred in the St. Paul wire text, and the wounded spectator is William Bluff in one and "a Mr. Ruff" in the other. The wire said the patrol wagon arrived before Luther was seriously hurt, while the Detroit dispatch said he was "terribly pounded and kicked" and half dead from fright. Luther's age is given as 54 in one report and 58 in the other.

accounts.label: Wire report (version 1)
accounts.gist: A brick struck Luther in the face, others wrenched away his revolver, and the crowd dragged him into the road with cries of 'lynch him' until the patrol wagon arrived before he was seriously hurt.

accounts.label: Wire report (version 2)
accounts.gist: The crowd seized Luther and was only prevented from lynching him on the spot by a large force of police who took him to jail.

accounts.label: Detroit dispatch of Dec. 19
accounts.gist: A crowd of leading merchants, bankers and lawyers threw bricks, yelled for a rope, and had a noose made from awning ropes; the sheriff, two deputies and police arrived and took away Luther, terribly beaten and bloodied.

framing.detail: The St. Paul Daily Globe headed the wire 'Luther Deserves Lynching' and called him 'the murderous man' and 'the would-be assassin'.

The Owosso Times, under 'Almost a Lynching', described the crowd as respectable men who 'did not seem to be aware of what they were doing' and joked that Luther 'might have ornamented a telegraph pole'.
Most papers ran the wire under headlines about the shooting ('Exciting Shooting Affray', 'Mad With Rage', 'Was a Poor Shot', 'Cowardly Husband and Father'), with the near-lynching as a closing line.
